result:
REST: resources at URLs, HTTP verbs, status codes. Strengths: HTTP caching (CDN, ETags) works out of the box, simple tooling (curl, browser), per-endpoint rate limiting and monitoring trivial, easy for public/third-party consumers. Weaknesses: over-fetching (fixed response shapes) and under-fetching (N round trips for related data), versioning pain as clients diverge, contract only as good as your OpenAPI discipline.

GraphQL: one endpoint, client specifies exact shape, strongly typed schema. Strengths: one request fetches nested data → fewer round trips (big win for mobile/varied frontends), schema = enforced contract + introspection + codegen, additive evolution without versions (deprecate fields). Costs: HTTP caching mostly lost (POST to one URL) → need client caches (Apollo, Relay) or persisted queries; server complexity: N+1 resolver problem → DataLoader batching; security surface: arbitrary query depth/cost → need depth limits, cost analysis, or allowlisted queries; errors return 200 with `errors` array → monitoring harder; file uploads awkward.

Verdict: REST for public APIs, simple CRUD, cache-heavy or read-mostly traffic, small teams. GraphQL when multiple clients need different views of interconnected data and you control the clients (persisted queries close most of the security/caching gap). Middle ground worth considering: REST + OpenAPI codegen, or tRPC if TypeScript end to end.
